title: Lettre Tate (mai 66) (Cristaux) : lettre (1966), tapuscrit (s.d.), notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting (from the previous page): A is a complete DVR with fraction field K and residue field k of characteristic p>0. E_K is an elliptic curve over K, and the object of study is the p-adic Galois module T_p(E_{\bar K}).

Case a), good ordinary reduction, continued. There is a canonical extension of Z_p[G_K]-modules 0 -> L^vee(1) -> T_p(E) -> L -> 0, where L is an unramified rank-1 Z_p-module (the etale quotient) and L^vee(1) is the connected (multiplicative) part. Its class lies in H^1(K, L^{-2}(1)). When the residue field is algebraically closed, Kummer theory identifies H^1(K, Z_p(1)) with the p-adic completion of K^*. The class then lies in L_0^{-2} ⊗ (K^*)^ = Hom(L_0^{⊗2}, (K^*)^).

The first lines of this page record the 'well-known' fact that, for good ordinary reduction, the class lies in the subgroup Hom_{Z_p}(L^2, A^{**}) ≅ L^{-2} ⊗ A^{**}. Here A^{**} = 1 + m_A, the principal units ('Einseinheiten'). In modern terms this is the Serre–Tate parameter q(E) ∈ Hom(T_pE_k ⊗ T_pE_k, \hat G_m(A)): the extension of p-divisible groups over A, restricted to the generic fibre, gives a Kummer class with unit (indeed principal-unit) value.

The bracketed N.B. explains why this makes sense. Exponentiation of a principal unit by a p-adic integer is well defined (u^a is determined mod p^n by a mod p^n), so 1+m is a Z_p-module.

The right-margin N.B. says the extension T_p(E_K) can be trivial (split). In modern terms this happens precisely for the Serre–Tate canonical lift (q = 1), which has CM. A partly illegible clause mentions 'd'indice fini' and 'hypersingulière'. The left margin says that in any case one gets an abelian action (presumably of inertia or Galois on the graded pieces).

Case b), good supersingular ('hypersingulière') reduction. Grothendieck states a conjectural dichotomy: either T_p(E) is semisimple (CM-type / formal CM case), or the image of π_1(K) in Aut(T_p(E_{\bar K})) is an open subgroup ('??').

Case (a'+b'), potentially good reduction. The j-invariant is integral, so after a finite extension of K one has good reduction, either ordinary (a') or supersingular (b'). He then remarks on the structure of the action of π_1 (an 'abelian'-type statement in the potentially ordinary case). For b'), the conjecture of b) implies the analogous statement for potentially supersingular curves.

The next page treats the non-potentially-good (multiplicative/Tate curve) case. There the Kummer class has nonzero image in Z_p under the valuation, so the extension does not come from p-divisible groups over A.
errors: No substantive mathematical error visible. 'Hom(L^2, A^{**})' should be read as Hom(L^{⊗2}, 1+m_A), and the identification with the Kummer class requires an algebraically closed (or at least suitably large) residue field, which the previous page assumes.

The right-margin phrase reads 'contrairement à Serre' or similar. If it means Serre expected non-splitness, note that the split case is exactly the canonical lift with CM, so there is no contradiction with Serre's later results for non-CM curves over number fields.

ideas.what: Extension class of the ordinary T_p(E) as a Kummer class lying in principal units 1+m_A (twisted by L^{-2})
ideas.modern_name: Serre–Tate parameter / canonical coordinates q(E) ∈ Hom(T_pE_k ⊗ T_pE_k^t, \hat G_m(A))
ideas.usually_credited_to: Serre–Tate (Woods Hole 1964), Katz 'Serre–Tate local moduli' (1981), Messing (1972)
ideas.where_published: Grothendieck himself calls it 'bien connu'; cf. Grothendieck's 1970 Nice ICM talk and 'Groupes de Barsotti–Tate et cristaux de Dieudonné' (1974) for related p-divisible group deformation theory

ideas.what: Split extension possible for good ordinary reduction
ideas.modern_name: Canonical (quasi-canonical) lift; split local Galois representation iff q=1 (CM)

ideas.what: Conjecture for supersingular good reduction: T_p semisimple or image of Galois open in Aut(T_p)
ideas.modern_name: Open image / Lie algebra of Galois image for height-2 formal groups (formal CM dichotomy)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Serre, 'Sur les groupes de Galois attachés aux groupes p-divisibles' (1967); Sen (1973); Serre, Propriétés galoisiennes (1972)

ideas.what: Reduction of the potentially good case to the good case after finite base extension
ideas.modern_name: Potentially good reduction; semistable/crystalline after finite extension
ideas.where_published: SGA 7 I (ℓ-adic monodromy); the p-adic analogue only as a program

missed.claim: Grothendieck formulated in private notes the dichotomy (semisimple vs open image) for the p-adic Tate module of a supersingular elliptic curve over a local field. This is essentially what Serre proved for formal groups of height 2 (1967) and Sen generalized (1973). It is an independent anticipation, not a missed result.
missed.quote: soit que l'image de π_1(K) dans Aut(T_p(E_{\bar K})) est un sous-groupe ouvert ... ??
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical only: it documents Grothendieck's parallel thinking on p-adic Galois images in the crystals/Tate-letter period. The mathematics is fully established.

deep.surprise_reason: The page sketches known material: the Serre–Tate parameter as a principal-unit Kummer class, canonical lifts giving split extensions, and a conjecture matching Serre/Sen open-image results for supersingular reduction. Grothendieck himself labels the main fact 'bien connu'. Interesting as a record of his thinking on p-adic Galois representations, but nothing new to specialists.
transcription_corrections: 'Einseinheiten' under A^{**} is correct: the German term for principal units 1+m_A.

'(a'+b') E_K n'a pas {mauvaise} réduction' should read 'n'a pas bonne réduction, mais [potentiellement] bonne réduction'. The inserted word above 'bonnes' is likely 'nécessairement' or 'pas nécessairement', not 'mauvaise'.
'unitabélienne' is uncertain; possibly 'quasi-abélienne' or 'unipotente'; should be marked illegible.
In the right-margin N.B., 'contrairement à Serre' is uncertain; the word may be 'conjecturalement' or a reference to a Serre remark.
